raw_response:
Aiya, what's there to think about? I've been growing chili on this little plot for forty years. Same as last year, same as the year before. Just me and the old man at home now — the kids are off in the city, only come back for the New Year. 2.6 mu of chili keeps the two of us busy enough.

I'll go to old Wang's nursery in the village around Labor Day to buy seedlings, like always. He grows the red ones everyone here plants — a few yuan a tray. I plant them out after the holiday when the cold won't come back. I lay plastic mulch on the ridges first — saves water, keeps the weeds down, and the soil stays warm. The plastic costs a bit but it's worth it, my back can't take all that weeding anymore.

For fertilizer, before planting I put down maybe three bags of compound fertilizer — what they call 15-15-15 at the agro-shop. The shopkeeper carries the bags out to my electric tricycle. When the chili starts setting fruit in July, I throw on a bag of urea, scatter it between the rows before watering. That's what my mother-in-law taught me, that's what everyone does. If the leaves look yellow I add a bit more, if they look dark green I save the money.

Water — chili drinks a lot. I share the well-pump with three neighbors down the lane, we take turns and split the electric bill. I water maybe six or seven times through the season, more if July is dry. The electricity isn't cheap but without water there's no chili.

Pests — every year the aphids come, and when August gets humid the fruits start rotting on the plant (the agro-shop man calls it 炭疽病). I spray four or five times. I just tell the shopkeeper "my chili has bugs" or "the fruits have black spots" and he picks the bottle for me. I can't read the labels but I remember the colors.

Picking is the hardest part. From early July until the first frost in October, every five or six days we go through and pick. My old man helps when his legs are good. During the busiest weeks in August my daughter sometimes brings her husband down for a weekend, or I pay a neighbor woman 80 yuan a day to help. Last year I sold maybe 5000 jin of fresh chili off the whole plot, plus some I dried on the roof and sold to the dried-chili man in winter. Got a fair price — not great, not terrible.

If the price is good I'll have some money left over after paying for the inputs. If it's bad, well, we eat what we grow and wait for next year.
